newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Holderbank keeps veil on restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Holderbank keeps veil on restructuring.

text.p: International cement and concrete maker Holderbank Financiere Glarus AG said on Thursday it would not detail for now its announced plans for cutting capacity in sated European markets.
Holderbank last week took a surprise one-time charge of 607 million Swiss francs for restructuring in the next two to three years, including closing one of five cement factories in Switzerland.
But Holderbank executives on Thursday were tight-lipped about plans for the rest of the special provisions after 161 million francs for closing the Swiss plant in early 1998.
"We have a clear idea of what we will do but we cannot talk about it yet," executive board member Urs Bieri told a news conference on the group's 1996 results.

Asked whether more plants would be closed, chief executive Thomas Schmidheiny said he would not comment now because the company was looking at exactly where to cut fixed costs and because the workforce at any targeted plant would have to be informed first.
But Schmidheiny made clear Holderbank, the world's leading cement maker, believed it must reduce capacity to cut costs in western Europe in particular.
"Based on our experience, we see a certain need to redimension and concentrate operations," Schmidheiny said.
"It is our view that western Europe is not just at a cyclical low but that it has a structural problem," he added.
Holderbank had closed about 15 plants in Europe over the past 15 years, he added, saying the current restructuring was a continuation of constant efforts to maintain cost leadership.
Schmidheiny reiterated that the company expected the next two to three years of European restructuring to reduce fixed costs by 50 million Swiss francs a year, a goal it announced last week.
"We are confident of succeeding in cutting fixed costs this way and strengtheneing our earnings potential," Schmidheiny told the news conference.

Schmidheiny said demand in Europe and Switzerland, which together account for about half of group sales, had declined sharply for lack of major infrastructure needs and would remain much lower than during construction booms in the 1970s and 1980s.

For example, he said Swiss cement demand in the early 1970s rose steadily to a high of around six million tonnes per year but eased to 5.5 million tonnes in 1990 before slumping to 3.6 million tonnes last year.
"In the year 2000 demand can be expected to reach 3.5 million tonnes at best. Similar developements are likely in western Europe," he said.
By contrast, markets in North America and Latin America were very strong and Holderbank's growing presence in eastern Europe and Asia promised to keep it linked to rising construction activity there.
